text: Think about a way that most of us use AI today, you ask it to analyze, draft or research something or help you make a decision, and it can be extremely capable, and you might even give it permanent instructions, access to some files or a set of skills. But you usually still drive the work forward. You ask, AI responds, you review the results, and then you decide what happens next. Agents change that relationship. While an assistant helps you do the work, an agent can carry bounded work forward for you. So imagine you have finished a meeting and you want to follow up on the commitments that were made. An assistant could definitely read the transcript and even draft a follow-up email. But an agent could go further. It could read the transcript, identify the commitments, check the relevant project information, notice a missing detail, retrieve it, update the follow-up, prepare the next actions, and then ask you to approve anything consequential. With an agent, you don't have to operate every step in between manually. Now that idea of carrying work forward is the most useful way I know to understand what makes an AI agentic. It's also the distinction used in our curriculum between reusable assistants and the agentic systems with bounded autonomy. So how does that actually happen? A useful mental model is the agent loop. The agent starts with context. What does it know about the goal, the situation, the rules, and the information available? It then decides what should happen next. It can take an action like searching for information, analyzing a document, creating something, updating something, or asking a person for input, and then it observes what happened. Did the search return useful information? Did the action succeed? Did something unexpected happen? And does it now have enough information to continue? Based on that observation, it can then decide whether to continue, to adjust, or to stop. And then the loop can run again. That repeated cycle lets an agent work through a multi-step task without you having to provide a new instruction after every step. But now we got to talk about bounded delegation, because none of this means that we're giving AI unlimited freedom. An agent might only be allowed to read information and prepare drafts. It might need your approval before changing a record or sending a message. And it might stop whenever information is missing or a decision carries significant consequences. And that's why we think about agentic AI as bounded delegation. You are giving AI responsibility for a defined part of work, but within boundaries that you choose. And the goal with agents, therefore, is never maximum autonomy. The goal is to decide where AI can carry the work forward, where human judgment still matters, and where the system should stop and ask.
